description: We are a team of two engineering students combining expertise in hardware and software development. Our skills include embedded systems, PCB design, robotics, IoT, web development, backend development, and AI. We aim to build innovative, practical technology solutions through creativity, teamwork, and continuous learning.
summary:
Still Here is an interactive website about three machines NASA sent beyond Earth: Spirit on Mars, Apollo 15’s rover on the Moon, and Voyager 1 in deep space.

Visitors explore a 3D solar system, pick a mission, and assemble its hardware as they scroll. Then they get to investigate for themselves. On Mars, they decide where Spirit should measure a dusty rock and compare real NASA photos to see why the rover ground into it. On the Moon, they learn why astronauts needed a car to find rocks that could tell us about the Moon’s past. In deep space, they search for Earth in Voyager’s Pale Blue Dot photo.

We built Still Here to help students explore NASA’s archives through questions they can answer themselves. Spirit and the lunar rover stayed behind, but what they helped us learn is still here.
details:
• What we built: Still Here is an interactive web exhibit about Spirit, Apollo 15’s lunar rover, and Voyager 1. Visitors choose a mission in a 3D solar system and see how its rover or spacecraft fits together as they scroll.
  • What makes it creative: Visitors get a clue to investigate in each story. They compare NASA photos of a Martian rock before and after Spirit ground into it, follow Apollo 15’s rover tracks, or search for Earth in Voyager’s Pale Blue Dot photo.
  • Who it helps: We designed the exhibit for students who are new to NASA’s mission archives. Short quizzes and open-ended questions help them explain how a photo, rock sample, or measurement can answer a scientific question.
  • Tools we used: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Vite, and Three.js. The exhibit runs in a web browser without special hardware.
  • What we considered: We used plain language, credited NASA imagery, and included keyboard controls and a reduced-motion option. In Spirit’s story, we made clear what visitors can see in the photos and what the rover needed instruments to measure.
